lesson.title: Dont & Où
lesson.subtitle: dont ('of which / whose') for de-verbs and où as relative 'where/when'.

hook.title: Completing the Relative Quartet: qui, que, dont, où
hook.content: Alongside qui (subject) and que (direct object), dont ('of which / whose / about which') steps in whenever the verb or phrase uses de (parler de → le film dont je parle; avoir besoin de → la chose dont j'ai besoin), and où ('where / when') steps in for BOTH places (la ville où j'habite) AND time nouns (le jour où il est arrivé)!

footnotes.title: Why French says 'le jour où' ('the day where') instead of '*le jour quand'
footnotes.content: After a time noun like le jour ('the day') or le moment ('the moment'), French treats time as a space and uses où ('where'): le jour où je t'ai vu!

pattern.title: de-Verb → dont; Place or Time Noun → où
pattern.content: Choose dont for de-constructions and où for places and time moments.
pattern.linguist_note: Relative adverb où (< Latin ubi) relativizes both spatial and temporal adjuncts, while dont (< dē unde) relativizes de-complements.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *le jour quand for 'the day when' — French always says le jour où!

exercises.prompt: Match each relative pronoun from the 4-word quartet with its trigger:

matching_pairs.english: que / qu' (Le livre que je lis)
matching_pairs.german: Direct object of the following clause
Replaces a de-phrase (parler de, avoir besoin de)

matching_pairs.english: où (La ville où j'habite / Le jour où...)
matching_pairs.german: Place ('where') OR Time ('when' after le jour/moment)

exercises.target_answer: Subject of the following verb, Direct object of the following clause, Replaces a de-phrase (parler de, avoir besoin de), Place ('where') OR Time ('when' after le jour/moment)
exercises.meaning: qui (L'ami qui arrive), que / qu' (Le livre que je lis), dont (Le livre dont j'ai besoin), où (La ville où j'habite / Le jour où...)
exercises.explanation: qui, que, dont, où form the complete 4-piece relative toolkit of French.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'That is the thing that I need' (remembering that 'to need' is 'avoir besoin DE')?
options: C'est la chose que j'ai besoin
C'est la chose dont j'ai besoin
C'est la chose dont j'en ai besoin
exercises.target_answer: C'est la chose dont j'ai besoin
exercises.meaning: That is the thing (of which) I have need
exercises.explanation: Because avoir besoin DE takes de, the relative pronoun is dont.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'the day when we arrived'?
options: le jour quand nous sommes arrivés
le jour que nous sommes arrivés
le jour où nous sommes arrivés
exercises.target_answer: le jour où nous sommes arrivés
exercises.meaning: the day when (lit. where) we arrived
exercises.explanation: After time nouns like le jour or le moment, French uses où for 'when'!

exercises.idea: this is the city where I lived (use C'est la ville où j'habitais)
cues: This is the city → C'est la ville
idea_parts: pointer + head noun → C'est la ville
exercises.meaning: This is the city where I used to live
exercises.explanation: où (with grave accent) links la ville to j'habitais.

diagnosis.cue: Use accented où ('where') after la ville.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Voici le restaurant dont je t'ai parlé
exercises.target_answer: Voici le restaurant dont je t'ai parlé
exercises.meaning: Here is the restaurant I told you about
exercises.affirmation: You used dont with je t'ai parlé cleanly!

summary.outcome: Deploy the complete relative pronoun system (qui, que, dont, où) across subjects, objects, de-verbs, places, and time nouns.

use_example.german: Le jour où je suis arrivé dans la ville dont tu parles.
use_example.english: The day when I arrived in the city you're talking about.

summary.takeaway: de-verb → dont; place or 'the day when' → où.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5101] Tout le conditionnel): see how Dont & Où leads directly into Tout le conditionnel.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "This is the city where I used to live" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "C'est la ville où j'habitais" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Dont & Où.

dont.context_phrase: C'est le film dont je parle.
dont.context_translation: That's the film I'm talking about (lit. of which I speak).
dont.etymology_derivation: Whenever the verb takes de (parler de, avoir besoin de), French uses dont.

où.etymology_derivation: Latin ubi 'where' — the root English borrowed wholesale in 'ubiquitous' (present everywhere).

qui.context_phrase: L'homme qui parle est mon père.
qui.context_translation: The man who is speaking is my father.
qui.etymology_derivation: Followed directly by the verb. Never drops its i before a vowel!

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

besoin.context_translation: I need help (lit. I have need of help).
besoin.etymology_derivation: Triggers dont in relative clauses because of its built-in de.

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

moment.etymology_derivation: Latin momentum 'movement, weight that tips the scales'. Noun in -ment is masculine.

livre.etymology_derivation: Masculine le livre is 'the book'; feminine la livre is 'the pound'!
